section: Scotland: SQA maths exam climb (National 4 skills, National 5, Higher, Advanced Higher)

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) start here: check and plan
lessons.intention: We are finding out which of the National 4 skills topics are already secure and which to learn first, and making a plan.
criteria: I can try one exam question on each of the 14 National 4 skills topics.
I know which topics I will work on first, and why.
I know how each topic works: lesson, online practice, exam-style sheet, then mini papers.

steps.start: Talk about the goal: the skills National 5 takes for granted, so the National 5 course itself is about National 5.
steps.teach: Explain the stage: 14 topics in order, each with a lesson, online practice and an exam-style sheet; mini papers every few sessions. Do the National 4 check (online or on paper), with a calculator but no help: it is a map, not a test.
steps.practise: The "SQA maths climb: National 4 check" sheet, or the online National 4 check.
steps.check: Mark the check together and fill in the "SQA maths climb: National 4 tracker" sheet: the topics that lost marks go first, in climb order.

lessons.home: Look at the tracker together and agree a weekly time for online practice.
lessons.vocab: course, paper, marking instructions, bullet, follow-through, secure
lessons.understand: Why work through the topics in the climb's order rather than starting with the hardest?
lessons.lookFor: Says the early topics are used inside the later ones, so they make the later topics easier as well as earning marks.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 1: Whole numbers, negatives, rounding and significant figures
lessons.intention: We are learning to read the value of any digit, put numbers in order (including decimals and negatives), round and estimate, as the exam asks.
criteria: I can say what any digit is worth, and order decimals by their place value.
I can add, subtract and find the difference with negative numbers in context.
I can round to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000, to decimal places and to 1 significant figure.
I can estimate a calculation by rounding each number to 1 significant figure.

steps.start: Which is bigger, 0.5 or 0.45? Ask for a reason, not a guess.
steps.teach: Use a place value grid for 0.6, 0.58 and 0.507: compare tenths first, so more digits is not bigger. Put −8 and −3 on a number line: further left is smaller. For a difference across zero, count to 0 and on. Round by looking only at the next digit; for 1 significant figure, find the first non-zero digit. Estimating: round every number to 1 significant figure first, then work it out; an exact answer to an "estimate" question scores nothing.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 1: Whole numbers, negatives, rounding and significant figures" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to estimate 49.2 × 3.8 and explain each step.

lessons.home: Spot temperatures below zero in a weather app and work out differences between two places.
lessons.vocab: digit, place value, decimal place, significant figure, estimate, negative
lessons.understand: Why is 0.507 smaller than 0.58, even though it has more digits?
lessons.lookFor: Compares the tenths first (5 tenths in both), then the hundredths (0 against 8); talks about place value, not the number of digits.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 2: Calculating without a calculator
lessons.intention: We are learning to multiply, divide and work with decimals by written methods, follow the order of operations, and make sense of remainders.
criteria: I can multiply a 3-digit number by a 2-digit number with a written method.
I can divide by a single digit with short division.
I can add, subtract and multiply decimals.
I can use the order of operations, and decide what a remainder means in a problem.

steps.start: Work out 5 + 3 × 4. Two people get 32 and 17: who is right?
steps.teach: Paper 1 has no calculator, so a reliable written method is worth many marks. Model the grid method and column multiplication for 247 × 36, writing the parts (247 × 30, 247 × 6) so a slip still earns method marks. Short division with remainders carried. Decimals: line up the points to add and subtract; to multiply, ignore the points, then put back the total number of decimal places. Order of operations: brackets, powers, × and ÷, + and −. A remainder in a problem: round up for buses and boxes needed, down for how many you can afford.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 2: Calculating without a calculator" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask for 318 × 24 with working, and how many 15-seat minibuses 82 people need.

lessons.home: Check a till receipt by adding it up on paper.
lessons.vocab: written method, partial product, remainder, decimal point, order of operations
lessons.understand: Why does 82 ÷ 15 = 5 remainder 7 mean 6 minibuses, not 5?
lessons.lookFor: Explains that the 7 left over still need a seat, so another minibus is needed; the answer must make sense in the story.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 3: Fractions and mixed numbers
lessons.intention: We are learning to find fractions of amounts, simplify, and add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions and mixed numbers.
criteria: I can find a fraction of an amount, and work backwards from a fraction to the whole.
I can simplify fractions and write one number as a fraction of another.
I can add and subtract fractions with different denominators.
I can multiply and divide fractions, and change between mixed numbers and improper fractions.

steps.start: Which is bigger, 3/5 or 5/8? How could you prove it?
steps.teach: Fraction of an amount: divide by the bottom, multiply by the top; going backwards, divide by the top to find one part. Simplify by dividing top and bottom by the same number. Add and subtract with a common denominator (never add the bottoms). Multiply: tops times tops, bottoms times bottoms. Divide: keep, change to ×, flip the second. Mixed numbers become improper fractions first. A bar model helps with every one of these.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 3: Fractions and mixed numbers" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask for 2/3 + 1/4, 3/5 of 45, and 2/3 of a number is 18: find the number.

lessons.home: Halve and third a recipe or a bill, and say the fractions.
lessons.vocab: numerator, denominator, simplest form, equivalent, common denominator, mixed number, improper fraction, reciprocal
lessons.understand: Why is 1/3 + 1/4 not 2/7?
lessons.lookFor: Explains that the parts must be the same size before they are added, so both become twelfths: 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 4: Percentages
lessons.intention: We are learning to change between fractions, decimals and percentages, find percentages of amounts, and work out increases, decreases, VAT, interest and percentage change.
criteria: I can change between fractions, decimals and percentages, and order them.
I can find a percentage of an amount without a calculator, building from 10%, 5% and 1%.
I can increase or decrease an amount by a percentage, including VAT and simple interest.
I can write one amount as a percentage of another and work out a percentage change.

steps.start: A shop takes 20% off, then another 20% off. Is that 40% off?
steps.teach: Percent means out of 100: 0.35 = 35/100 = 35%. Non-calculator: 10% (÷ 10), 5% (half of that), 1% (÷ 100), then build any percentage. Increase or decrease: find the percentage then add or take it away, or use a multiplier (a 15% decrease is × 0.85). VAT is 20%. Simple interest is the same amount each year. Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100: divide by the original, never the new amount.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 4: Percentages" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask for 35% of £160 without a calculator, and the percentage increase from £40 to £46.

lessons.home: Spot sale signs and work out the saving and the new price.
lessons.vocab: percentage, multiplier, increase, decrease, VAT, interest, original
lessons.understand: Why is a 20% reduction followed by another 20% reduction not 40% off?
lessons.lookFor: Explains that the second 20% is of the smaller, reduced price, so the total saving is less: × 0.8 × 0.8 = × 0.64, which is 36% off.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 5: Ratio and proportion
lessons.intention: We are learning to simplify and share in a ratio, scale recipes, find best buys, use exchange rates and the unitary method.
criteria: I can simplify a ratio and link a ratio to fractions.
I can share an amount in a given ratio, and use a ratio when one part is known.
I can scale a recipe and use the unitary method.
I can compare best buys and use exchange rates, showing the working that justifies my choice.

steps.start: Two packs: 6 for £2.40 or 10 for £3.80. Which would you buy, and how do you know?
steps.teach: Simplify a ratio like a fraction: divide both parts by the same number. Sharing: add the parts, find one part, multiply. When one part is known (3 : 4 and 15 boys), find what one part is worth first. Recipes and the unitary method: find one, then scale. Best buy: work out the price of one (or the amount per £1) for both, and say which is better; the decision alone gets no marks. Exchange rates: multiply to go from pounds, divide to go back.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 5: Ratio and proportion" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to share £60 in the ratio 2 : 3, and to compare two packs of batteries.

lessons.home: Compare prices of two pack sizes on a shopping trip or website.
lessons.vocab: ratio, simplest form, share, proportion, unit price, best buy, exchange rate
lessons.understand: In a 2 : 5 ratio of boys to girls, why are 5/7 of the class girls and not 5/2?
lessons.lookFor: Explains that the whole class is 2 + 5 = 7 parts, so girls are 5 of the 7 parts.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 6: Expressions and formulae
lessons.intention: We are learning to simplify expressions, substitute into formulae, expand and factorise single brackets, and write expressions from words.
criteria: I can collect like terms and simplify products such as 4x × 3y.
I can substitute positive and negative numbers into expressions and formulae.
I can expand a single bracket and factorise by taking out a common factor.
I can write an expression from a description, and tell an expression, equation and formula apart.

steps.start: If a = 3, what is 2a? Some say 23. Why?
steps.teach: Like terms have the same letter part: 3a + 5b − a + 2b = 2a + 7b. Letters next to each other multiply. Substitute by writing the number in brackets in place of the letter, then follow the order of operations; take care with negatives. Expanding: multiply everything inside the bracket. Factorising is the reverse: take out the biggest common factor and check by expanding. An expression has no equals sign; an equation can be solved; a formula links quantities.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 6: Expressions and formulae" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask for 3(2x − 5) expanded, 6x + 9 factorised, and 4a + 3b when a = 3, b = −2.

lessons.home: Write a formula for a phone plan or taxi fare and use it.
lessons.vocab: term, like terms, expression, equation, formula, substitute, expand, factorise, coefficient
lessons.understand: Why can't 3a + 2b be simplified?
lessons.lookFor: Explains that a and b stand for different things, so they are not like terms and can't be added together.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 7: Equations and inequations
lessons.intention: We are learning to solve linear equations and inequalities, and find terms and the nth term of a linear sequence.
criteria: I can solve equations in one or two steps, and with brackets.
I can solve equations with the letter on both sides.
I can solve simple inequalities and list the whole numbers that fit.
I can continue a sequence, find the nth term of a linear sequence, and decide if a number is in it.

steps.start: I think of a number, multiply by 3 and add 5. I get 26. What was my number?
steps.teach: Solving is undoing, keeping both sides balanced: write each step on a new line (each line can earn a mark). Brackets: expand first or divide both sides. Letters on both sides: take away the smaller number of letters first. Inequalities solve the same way; < means "not including" and ≤ "including", so −2 < n ≤ 3 is −1, 0, 1, 2, 3. Sequences: find the difference, that's the number in front of n, then adjust to match the first term. To test if a number is in a sequence, solve nth term = number: a whole number n means yes.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 7: Equations and inequations" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to solve 5x − 3 = 2x + 9, and find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14.

lessons.home: Make up an "I think of a number" puzzle for someone at home to solve.
lessons.vocab: solve, equation, inequality, integer, sequence, term, nth term, difference
lessons.understand: Why does the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14 start with 3n?
lessons.lookFor: Says the terms go up by 3 each time, the same as the 3 times table, so 3n; then + 2 makes the first term 5.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 8: Coordinates, straight-line graphs and gradient
lessons.intention: We are learning to use coordinates and midpoints, read and draw straight-line graphs, and use y = mx + c and real-life graphs.
criteria: I can plot and read coordinates in all four quadrants, and find a midpoint.
I can complete a table of values and draw a straight-line graph.
I can find the gradient and y-intercept from y = mx + c, and recognise horizontal and vertical lines.
I can read values from real-life graphs and use them to answer questions.

steps.start: Does the point (2, 7) lie on the line y = 3x + 1? How can you check without drawing it?
steps.teach: Coordinates: along the corridor, then up the stairs. Midpoint: add the x's and halve, add the y's and halve. Table of values: substitute each x, including negatives. In y = mx + c, m is the gradient (up for each 1 across) and c is where it crosses the y-axis. y = 4 is horizontal, x = 4 vertical. Reading a graph: go up from the x value to the line, then across; use a ruler and write the reading. Real-life graphs: the start is the fixed charge, the gradient is the rate.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 8: Coordinates, straight-line graphs and gradient" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask for the midpoint of (2, 4) and (8, 10) and the gradient of y = 4x − 3.

lessons.home: Find a taxi or delivery charge with a fixed fee and a rate, and sketch its graph.
lessons.vocab: coordinate, axis, midpoint, gradient, intercept, linear, horizontal, vertical
lessons.understand: In a plumber's charge of £35 plus £20 an hour, what do the 35 and the 20 mean on the graph?
lessons.lookFor: Says 35 is where the line starts on the y-axis (the charge for 0 hours) and 20 is the gradient, how much it goes up for each hour.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 9: Time, speed and measurement
lessons.intention: We are learning to convert metric and simple imperial units, work with time and timetables, and use speed, distance and time.
criteria: I can convert between metric units of length, mass and capacity.
I can work with 12- and 24-hour times and find durations.
I can change decimal hours into hours and minutes.
I can use speed = distance ÷ time to find speed, distance or time.

steps.start: A film lasts 1.5 hours. Is that 1 hour 50 minutes?
steps.teach: Learn the metric facts (1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 litre = 1000 ml) and multiply to smaller units, divide to bigger ones. Area and volume units are squared and cubed: 1 m² = 10 000 cm². Time is not decimal: count on to the next hour, then on, for durations; 0.25 hours is 15 minutes. Speed: the formula triangle, with time in hours (20 minutes = 1/3 hour). 5 miles ≈ 8 km.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 9: Time, speed and measurement" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask for the time between 14:47 and 16:15, and the speed for 150 miles in 2 hours 30 minutes.

lessons.home: Plan a journey from a real bus or train timetable.
lessons.vocab: metric, convert, duration, 24-hour clock, speed, average, km/h, mph
lessons.understand: Why is 2.25 hours not 2 hours 25 minutes?
lessons.lookFor: Explains there are 60 minutes in an hour, so 0.25 of an hour is a quarter of 60, which is 15 minutes.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 10: Angles, shapes, bearings and scale
lessons.intention: We are learning to use angle facts on lines, around points and in triangles, quadrilaterals and polygons, parallel line angles, shape properties and bearings, giving reasons.
criteria: I can use angles on a straight line, around a point, in a triangle and in a quadrilateral.
I can use isosceles triangle facts and angles in regular polygons.
I can name alternate, corresponding and co-interior angles and use them, giving reasons.
I can name shapes from their properties and read bearings.

steps.start: What do the angles in a triangle add up to? Can you show it by tearing the corners off?
steps.teach: The facts: straight line 180°, around a point 360°, triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, polygon (n − 2) × 180°, exterior angles of any polygon 360°. Isosceles: two equal angles at the base. Parallel lines: alternate (Z) equal, corresponding (F) equal, co-interior (C) add to 180°. In the exam, write the reason next to each step using the proper wording: the reasons carry marks. Bearings: from north, clockwise, three figures.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 10: Angles, shapes, bearings and scale" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask for each interior angle of a regular hexagon, with reasons.

lessons.home: Find angles and parallel lines in a road junction, a window frame or a bike.
lessons.vocab: angle, straight line, isosceles, polygon, interior, exterior, parallel, alternate, corresponding, bearing
lessons.understand: Why do you have to write a reason for each angle in the exam?
lessons.lookFor: Says the question asks you to show you know why, and the reasons themselves earn marks.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 11: Area, volume and circles
lessons.intention: We are learning to find perimeters and areas of rectangles, triangles, parallelograms, trapeziums, compound shapes and circles, and volumes and surface areas of cuboids.
criteria: I can find the perimeter and area of rectangles and compound shapes.
I can find the area of triangles, parallelograms and trapeziums.
I can find the area and circumference of a circle with a calculator.
I can find the volume and surface area of a cuboid, and solve problems with them.

steps.start: A rectangle has an area of 24 cm². How many different whole-number perimeters can it have?
steps.teach: Perimeter is the distance round; area is the space inside, in square units. Triangle: ½ × base × perpendicular height. Parallelogram: base × perpendicular height. Trapezium: ½(a + b)h (it is on the formula sheet in some years, but learn it). Compound shapes: find the missing sides first, then split or subtract. Circle: area πr², circumference πd; use the π button and round only at the end. Cuboid volume: l × w × h; surface area: add the six faces. In problems, round up tins and boxes.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 11: Area, volume and circles" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask for the area of an L-shape and the number of paint tins for a wall.

lessons.home: Measure a room and work out the floor area and how much flooring it needs.
lessons.vocab: perimeter, area, perpendicular height, compound, radius, diameter, circumference, π, volume, surface area
lessons.understand: Why does a triangle's area use half of base × height?
lessons.lookFor: Explains that a triangle is half of a rectangle (or parallelogram) with the same base and height.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 12: Pythagoras' theorem
lessons.intention: We are learning to use Pythagoras' theorem to find any side of a right-angled triangle, and in context.
criteria: I can find the longest side (hypotenuse) of a right-angled triangle.
I can find a shorter side.
I can check whether a triangle is right-angled.
I can use Pythagoras for the distance between two points and in real problems.

steps.start: A 5 m ladder, foot 3 m from the wall: how high does it reach? Let them try before teaching.
steps.teach: Label the hypotenuse first: it is opposite the right angle and always the longest. Longest side: square the two shorter sides, add, square root. Shorter side: square the longest, subtract the other square, square root. Check the answer: the hypotenuse must be the longest. For two points, draw the right-angled triangle across and up.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 12: Pythagoras' theorem" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to explain how they know whether to add or subtract the squares.

lessons.home: Measure a door or a TV screen and check the diagonal with Pythagoras.
lessons.vocab: hypotenuse, right angle, square, square root, Pythagoras' theorem
lessons.understand: How do you know whether to add or subtract the squares?
lessons.lookFor: Says add when finding the longest side (hypotenuse) and subtract when finding a shorter one.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 13: Right-angled trigonometry
lessons.intention: We are learning to use sin, cos and tan to find sides and angles in right-angled triangles, and the exact values to know.
criteria: I can label the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse from an angle.
I can choose sin, cos or tan with SOH CAH TOA.
I can find a missing side and a missing angle.
I know the exact values of sin, cos and tan for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°.

steps.start: Show two right-angled triangles with the same angles but different sizes. Ask what stays the same.
steps.teach: From the marked angle, label the hypotenuse (longest), opposite (across from the angle) and adjacent (next to it). Tick the two sides involved and pick the ratio: SOH CAH TOA. For a side, multiply (or divide, if the unknown is on the bottom). For an angle, use the inverse key (sin⁻¹ and so on). Check the calculator is in degrees. Learn the exact values from the two special triangles.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 13: Right-angled trigonometry" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the angle in a triangle with opposite 5 cm and adjacent 8 cm, saying which ratio and why.

lessons.home: Use an angle and a distance to estimate the height of a tree or building.
lessons.vocab: sine, cosine, tangent, opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse, inverse
lessons.understand: Why do you use the inverse key to find an angle?
lessons.lookFor: Says sin, cos or tan of an angle gives a ratio, so the inverse takes the ratio back to the angle.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 4) 14: Statistics and probability
lessons.intention: We are learning to find and use the mean, median, mode and range, work with frequency tables and pie charts, and describe correlation, and to work out simple probabilities.
criteria: I can find the mean, median, mode and range of a list.
I can find a missing value when I know the mean.
I can find totals from a frequency table and angles for a pie chart.
I can find a probability as a fraction, and place it on the 0 to 1 scale.

steps.start: The mean of five numbers is 10. What could the numbers be? Is there only one answer?
steps.teach: Mean: add up and divide by how many. Median: put in order first, then the middle (halfway between the two middle ones if there's an even number). Mode: most common. Range: largest − smallest, a measure of spread. Missing value: the mean × how many gives the total. Frequency table: multiply each value by its frequency to get the total. Pie chart: 360° ÷ total gives the angle for each person. Correlation: positive, negative or none; it does not prove one thing causes the other. Probability: a value from 0 to 1, as a fraction or decimal; it is the number of ways the event can happen out of all the equally likely outcomes, and P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 4) 14: Statistics and probability" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask for the median of 7 unsorted numbers and the pie chart angle for 15 people out of 60.

lessons.home: Collect journey times for a week and find the mean, median and range.
lessons.vocab: mean, median, mode, range, frequency, pie chart, scatter graph, correlation
lessons.understand: Why do you have to put the numbers in order before finding the median?
lessons.lookFor: Explains that the median is the middle value by size, not by position in the list.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb: what National 5 expects (National 4 skills)
lessons.intention: We are learning how National 4 is passed, what National 5 assumes we can already do, and the habits of setting out working that SQA marking rewards.
criteria: I know National 4 is passed in school, with no exam.
I know each step of working earns its own mark (one bullet a mark).
I know an error is followed through, so I never leave a question blank.

steps.start: Show an answer with a slip in the middle. Ask how many marks it should keep.
steps.teach: Go through the "What National 5 expects: the National 4 skills" sheet, then mark its model answers together.
steps.practise: Mark the model answers on the "What National 5 expects: the National 4 skills" sheet together, then the online mixed exam questions with full working on paper.
steps.check: Ask them to explain follow-through, and what an answer with no working risks.

lessons.home: Do the online mixed exam questions, writing full working on paper.
lessons.vocab: paper, non-calculator, formulae list, bullet mark, follow-through, grade boundary
lessons.understand: Why can a wrong final answer still earn most of a question's marks?
lessons.lookFor: Says each step earns its own bullet, and steps after a slip still count when they're done correctly.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb: mini papers (National 4)
lessons.intention: We are practising exam questions from all the topics together, under exam conditions, and using the results to plan what to revise.
criteria: I can answer mixed exam questions without being told the topic.
I show my working on every question.
I can use my marks to choose which topics to go back to.

steps.start: Recap the habits: read twice, underline the command word, one step a line, round only at the end.
steps.teach: Set up exam conditions: about 20 minutes, quiet, calculator only for the calculator paper. Remind them to do the questions they can first.
steps.practise: One of the "Mini paper: non-calculator (SQA National 4)", "Mini paper: calculator (SQA National 4)" or "Mini paper: longer questions (SQA National 4)" sheets. Each print is a new paper.
steps.check: Mark it together the SQA way, then write the score and the topics to go back to on the tracker.

lessons.home: Redo the questions that lost marks, then the online mixed exam questions.
lessons.vocab: exam conditions, marking, topic, revise
lessons.understand: Your mini paper shows you lost marks on two topics. What do you do next?
lessons.lookFor: Goes back to those topics' lessons or exam sheets before the next mini paper, rather than just doing more papers.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) start here: check and plan
lessons.intention: We are finding out which of the National 5 topics are already secure and which to learn first, and making a plan.
criteria: I can try one exam question on each of the 14 National 5 topics.
I know which topics I will work on first, and why.
I know how each topic works: lesson, online practice, exam-style sheet, then mini papers.

steps.start: Talk about the goal: a pass at National 5 (and an A or B if Higher comes next). Most marks come from steps of working, not just answers.
steps.teach: Explain the stage: 14 topics in order, each with a lesson, online practice and an exam-style sheet; mini papers every few sessions. Do the National 5 check (online or on paper), with a calculator but no help: it is a map, not a test.
steps.practise: The "SQA maths climb: National 5 check" sheet, or the online National 5 check.
steps.check: Mark the check together and fill in the "SQA maths climb: National 5 tracker" sheet: the topics that lost marks go first, in climb order.

lessons.home: Look at the tracker together and agree a weekly time for online practice.
lessons.vocab: course, paper, marking instructions, bullet, follow-through, secure
lessons.understand: Why work through the topics in the climb's order rather than starting with the hardest?
lessons.lookFor: Says the early topics are used inside the later ones, so they make the later topics easier as well as earning marks.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 1: Surds, indices and scientific notation
lessons.intention: We are learning to simplify surds, rationalise denominators, use the laws of indices (including negative and fractional powers) and calculate in scientific notation.
criteria: I can simplify a surd such as √72 = 6√2, and add and subtract like surds.
I can rationalise a denominator.
I can use the laws of indices, including negative and fractional indices.
I can write numbers in scientific notation and calculate with them.

steps.start: Ask: is √8 + √2 the same as √10? Try it on a calculator, then find out why not.
steps.teach: Simplify a surd by taking out the biggest square factor: √72 = √36 × √2 = 6√2. Only like surds add. To rationalise, multiply top and bottom by the surd on the bottom. Laws of indices: add powers to multiply, subtract to divide, multiply for a power of a power; a⁰ = 1, a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, a^(1/n) is the nth root. Scientific notation: a number from 1 up to 10 times a power of 10; on Paper 2 use the calculator's ×10ˣ key, then write the answer properly (not the calculator's E).
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 1: Surds, indices and scientific notation" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to simplify √50 − √8 and to evaluate 27^(2/3) without a calculator.

lessons.home: Find the mass of the Earth and of an electron, and write the ratio in scientific notation.
lessons.vocab: surd, rationalise, index, power, reciprocal, root, scientific notation
lessons.understand: Why is √12 + √3 = 3√3, but √12 + √5 can't be simplified?
lessons.lookFor: Says √12 = 2√3, so it's like terms (2 lots of √3 plus 1), but √5 is a different surd.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 2: Percentages, appreciation and depreciation, and mixed numbers
lessons.intention: We are learning to work out appreciation and depreciation over several years, find the original amount before a percentage change, and calculate with mixed numbers.
criteria: I can use a multiplier for a percentage increase or decrease.
I can work out compound interest, appreciation and depreciation over several years.
I can find the original amount after a percentage change (reverse percentages).
I can add, subtract, multiply and divide mixed numbers.

steps.start: A car loses 15% of its value each year. Ask: after two years, has it lost 30%?
steps.teach: Every change is one multiplication: up 4% is × 1.04, down 15% is × 0.85; over n years, × 0.85ⁿ. To go back to the original, divide by the multiplier (a price after a 20% rise is 120%, so ÷ 1.2), never take 20% off. Mixed numbers: make them improper fractions; for + and − use a common denominator, for × multiply across, for ÷ flip the second and multiply; give the answer as a mixed number in its simplest form. Paper 1 can ask any of these without a calculator.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 2: Percentages, appreciation and depreciation, and mixed numbers" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the price before a 12% rise to £336, and to work out 2⅓ ÷ 1¾.

lessons.home: Look up the value of a used car now and new, and work out its average yearly depreciation.
lessons.vocab: multiplier, appreciation, depreciation, compound interest, original amount, mixed number, improper fraction
lessons.understand: Why is the original price of a £96 coat after 20% off not £96 + 20%?
lessons.lookFor: Says the 20% was of the original price, not £96: £96 is 80%, so the original is £96 ÷ 0.8 = £120.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 3: Expanding, factorising and completing the square
lessons.intention: We are learning to expand brackets (including a bracket times a trinomial), factorise fully and complete the square.
criteria: I can expand and simplify two brackets, and a bracket times a trinomial.
I can factorise with a common factor, a difference of two squares and a trinomial.
I can always check for a common factor first, to factorise fully.
I can write x² + bx + c in the form (x + p)² + q.

steps.start: Ask them to expand (x + 3)(x − 3) and (x + 3)², and spot the difference.
steps.teach: Expand every term by every term, then collect like terms; for (x + 2)(x² − 3x + 4) that's six terms. Factorise in this order: a common factor, then a difference of two squares (a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b)), then a trinomial (find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b; for 2x² + …, test the pairs). Check by expanding. Completing the square: halve the x coefficient for the bracket, then take away its square.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 3: Expanding, factorising and completing the square" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to factorise 2x² − 18 fully, and to write x² − 10x + 7 in the form (x + p)² + q.

lessons.home: Make a card sort: expressions on one set, their factorised forms on the other.
lessons.vocab: expand, factorise, common factor, difference of two squares, trinomial, completing the square
lessons.understand: Why is 2x² − 18 = (2x + 6)(x − 3) correct but not fully factorised?
lessons.lookFor: Says 2 is a common factor of 2x + 6, so it should be 2(x + 3)(x − 3).

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 4: Algebraic fractions
lessons.intention: We are learning to simplify algebraic fractions by factorising, and to add, subtract, multiply and divide them.
criteria: I can simplify an algebraic fraction by factorising and cancelling a common factor.
I can add and subtract algebraic fractions with a common denominator.
I can multiply and divide algebraic fractions.

steps.start: Ask: can you cancel the x in (x + 3)/x? Try x = 2.
steps.teach: Only whole factors cancel, never parts of a sum: factorise top and bottom first, then cancel a bracket that is on both. To add or subtract, find a common denominator (multiply the denominators), multiply each top by what its bottom was multiplied by, then combine; take care with a minus in front of a bracket. To multiply, multiply tops and bottoms; to divide, flip the second fraction and multiply, then cancel.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 4: Algebraic fractions" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to simplify (x² − 9)/(x² + x − 6) and to write 3/x − 2/(x + 1) as a single fraction.

lessons.home: Test a simplified fraction by putting in x = 5 before and after: the values should match.
lessons.vocab: algebraic fraction, factor, cancel, common denominator, simplest form
lessons.understand: Why can't you cancel the 3s in (x + 3)/3?
lessons.lookFor: Says the 3 on top is part of a sum (x + 3), not a factor of the whole top, so cancelling changes the value.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 5: Equations, inequations and changing the subject
lessons.intention: We are learning to solve linear equations and inequations (including with brackets and fractions) and to change the subject of a formula.
criteria: I can solve equations with brackets, letters on both sides and fractions.
I can solve an inequation, turning the sign when I multiply or divide by a negative.
I can change the subject of a formula, including ones with powers, roots and fractions.

steps.start: Ask: if −2x > 6, is x > −3? Try x = 0.
steps.teach: Do the same to both sides; clear brackets first, and clear fractions by multiplying every term by the denominator. Inequations work the same, except that multiplying or dividing by a negative turns the sign round. To change the subject, undo what has been done to the letter in reverse order: a square is undone by a square root, a fraction by multiplying.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 5: Equations, inequations and changing the subject" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to solve (2x + 1)/3 = x − 4 and to make r the subject of V = πr²h.

lessons.home: Find a formula from science (such as v = u + at) and change its subject two ways.
lessons.vocab: equation, inequation, solve, subject, inverse operation
lessons.understand: Why does the sign turn round when you divide an inequation by −2?
lessons.lookFor: Says it swaps which side is bigger, e.g. 4 > 2 but −2 < −1.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 6: Simultaneous equations
lessons.intention: We are learning to solve simultaneous equations by elimination and from a graph, and to form them from a problem.
criteria: I can solve simultaneous equations by elimination.
I can find the solution from where two lines cross.
I can form two equations from a problem in words and answer in context.

steps.start: Two coffees and a cake cost £8; one coffee and a cake cost £5.50. Ask for the cost of a coffee before any method.
steps.teach: Elimination: scale one or both equations so one letter has the same coefficient, then add or subtract to remove it; solve, then substitute back. Check in the other equation. On a graph, the solution is the point where the lines cross. In a problem, say what the letters stand for, form both equations, and finish with a sentence in context. SQA marks: forming the equations, eliminating, each value.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 6: Simultaneous equations" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to solve 3x + 2y = 16 and 2x − y = 6, and check in both.

lessons.home: Use two shopping receipts with the same items in different amounts to find each price.
lessons.vocab: simultaneous, eliminate, substitute, coefficient, point of intersection
lessons.understand: Why do the two equations need to be solved together, not one at a time?
lessons.lookFor: Says each equation alone has endless solutions; only one pair of values works in both.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 7: Straight lines and gradient
lessons.intention: We are learning to find gradients and the equation of a straight line in the forms y = mx + c and y − b = m(x − a).
criteria: I can find the gradient between two points.
I can find the gradient and y-intercept from an equation, rearranging if needed.
I can find the equation of a line from its gradient and a point, or from two points.

steps.start: Show the line 2y = 6x + 4. Ask: is its gradient 6?
steps.teach: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x (vertical ÷ horizontal). In y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c the y-intercept, so make y the subject first. Through a point (a, b) with gradient m: y − b = m(x − a), which SQA accepts as the answer unless a form is asked for. Parallel lines have equal gradients.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 7: Straight lines and gradient" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them for the equation of the line through (2, 5) and (6, 13).

lessons.home: Find a real gradient (a road sign's 10% or a ramp) and draw it to scale.
lessons.vocab: gradient, intercept, y = mx + c, parallel
lessons.understand: Why must 2y = 6x + 4 be divided by 2 before reading the gradient?
lessons.lookFor: Says y = mx + c needs y on its own, so y = 3x + 2 and the gradient is 3.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 8: Quadratic functions and equations
lessons.intention: We are learning to sketch and read parabolas, solve quadratic equations by factorising and the formula, and use the discriminant.
criteria: I can find the turning point and axis of symmetry from y = (x − a)² + b.
I can find the equation of a parabola from its graph.
I can solve a quadratic by factorising or by the quadratic formula.
I can use the discriminant to state the nature of the roots.

steps.start: Ask: where does y = (x − 2)² + 1 reach its lowest point, and how do you know?
steps.teach: y = (x − a)² + b has its turning point at (a, b), a minimum if x² is positive and a maximum if negative; the axis of symmetry is x = a. To sketch: roots, y-intercept, turning point. Solve by making one side 0, then factorise; if it won't factorise (or the question asks for rounded answers), use the formula from the formulae list. The discriminant b² − 4ac: positive, two real distinct roots; zero, equal roots; negative, no real roots.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 8: Quadratic functions and equations" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to solve 2x² + 3x − 4 = 0 to 1 decimal place, and state the nature of the roots of x² + 4x + 5 = 0.

lessons.home: Photograph a curve shaped like a parabola (a bridge, a fountain) and estimate its turning point.
lessons.vocab: parabola, turning point, axis of symmetry, root, discriminant, quadratic formula
lessons.understand: How can you tell, without solving, that x² + 4x + 5 = 0 has no real roots?
lessons.lookFor: Works out b² − 4ac = 16 − 20 = −4, negative, so no real roots (the parabola doesn't cross the x-axis).

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 9: Pythagoras, angles and similarity
lessons.intention: We are learning to use Pythagoras in 2D and 3D and its converse, angle properties of polygons and circles in several steps, and similar shapes.
criteria: I can use Pythagoras in a 2D or 3D problem, including chords in circles.
I can use the converse of Pythagoras to decide if a triangle is right-angled.
I can find angles in several steps with reasons (polygons, tangents, semicircles).
I can use the scale factor of similar shapes for lengths, areas and volumes.

steps.start: Show a pipe with water in it. Ask how you could find the depth from the width of the surface.
steps.teach: In a circle, a radius to a tangent is at 90°, the angle in a semicircle is 90°, and a radius perpendicular to a chord bisects it: each gives a right-angled triangle for Pythagoras. Converse: if a² + b² = c², the angle is 90° (state it). For similar shapes: lengths scale by k, areas by k², volumes by k³.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 9: Pythagoras, angles and similarity" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to decide whether a 9, 12, 15 triangle is right-angled, and to find the area of a similar shape twice as long.

lessons.home: Measure a phone screen's width and height, and check its diagonal by Pythagoras.
lessons.vocab: Pythagoras, converse, hypotenuse, chord, tangent, similar, scale factor
lessons.understand: Why does a doubled photo need four times the paper?
lessons.lookFor: Says area scales by the square of the length scale factor: 2² = 4.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 10: Arcs, sectors and volumes
lessons.intention: We are learning to find arc lengths and sector areas, and the volumes of spheres, cones, pyramids and composite solids.
criteria: I can find an arc length and a sector area from the angle.
I can work backwards from an arc or sector to the angle.
I can find the volume of a sphere, cone, pyramid and prism.
I can find the volume of a composite solid and round sensibly.

steps.start: Ask: what fraction of a pizza is a slice with a 60° angle? So what fraction of the crust?
steps.teach: Arc length = angle/360 × πd; sector area = angle/360 × πr². Volumes: sphere 4/3πr³, cone 1/3πr²h, pyramid 1/3 × base area × height (on the formulae list), cylinder πr²h. For composite solids, add or subtract parts; keep full values on the calculator and round only at the end, to the accuracy asked (often 3 significant figures).
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 10: Arcs, sectors and volumes" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the volume of a cone of radius 4 cm and height 9 cm, and the angle of a sector with arc 10 cm and radius 6 cm.

lessons.home: Measure a ball and estimate its volume; then fill a jug to check.
lessons.vocab: arc, sector, sphere, cone, pyramid, composite, significant figures
lessons.understand: Why is a cone's volume a third of a cylinder's with the same base and height?
lessons.lookFor: Says three cones' worth fill the cylinder (shown by filling, or by the formula 1/3πr²h).

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 11: Trigonometry: area, sine rule, cosine rule and bearings
lessons.intention: We are learning to use the sine rule, the cosine rule and ½ab sin C in triangles without a right angle, and bearings.
criteria: I can choose the sine rule, the cosine rule or the area formula from what I know.
I can find a side or an angle with the sine and cosine rules.
I can find a triangle's area with ½ab sin C.
I can solve bearings problems with these rules.

steps.start: Show a triangle with no right angle. Ask: can SOH CAH TOA find the third side?
steps.teach: Label sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C. Area = ½ab sin C (two sides and the angle between). Sine rule (pairs of side and opposite angle): use it when you know a side and its opposite angle. Cosine rule: two sides and the angle between, to find the third side, or three sides to find an angle. All are on the formulae list. For bearings, draw north lines and use parallel-line angles to find the angle in the triangle.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 11: Trigonometry: area, sine rule, cosine rule and bearings" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the area of a triangle with sides 7 cm and 9 cm and an angle of 50° between them, then the third side.

lessons.home: Use a map to find the bearing and distance between two towns, then check with the cosine rule.
lessons.vocab: sine rule, cosine rule, included angle, bearing, area
lessons.understand: How do you choose between the sine rule and the cosine rule?
lessons.lookFor: Says the sine rule needs a side and its opposite angle; otherwise, with two sides and the angle between or three sides, use the cosine rule.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 12: Trigonometric graphs, equations and identities
lessons.intention: We are learning to read and sketch trig graphs, solve trig equations from 0° to 360°, and simplify with the trig identities.
criteria: I can state the amplitude and period of y = a sin bx° and y = a cos bx°.
I can find the equation of a trig graph that is stretched or moved.
I can solve a trig equation, finding all the solutions from 0° to 360°.
I can simplify with sin²x + cos²x = 1 and tan x = sin x / cos x.

steps.start: Ask: sin 30° = 0.5. Is there another angle under 360° with sine 0.5?
steps.teach: y = a sin bx°: amplitude a (the maximum), b waves in 360°, so the period is 360° ÷ b. y = sin(x − c)° moves the graph c° right. To solve, rearrange to sin x° = k, find the calculator's angle, then use the quadrant diagram (All, Sin, Tan, Cos) to find the second solution in 0° to 360°. Identities: replace sin²x + cos²x with 1, and sin x / cos x with tan x.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 12: Trigonometric graphs, equations and identities" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to solve 4 cos x° + 1 = −1 for 0 ≤ x < 360, and to simplify sin x° / tan x°.

lessons.home: Sketch the graph of daylight hours over a year and say what its period is.
lessons.vocab: amplitude, period, phase, quadrant, identity
lessons.understand: Why does 2 sin x° = 1 have two solutions between 0° and 360°?
lessons.lookFor: Says sine is positive in two quadrants (first and second), so x = 30° and 180° − 30° = 150°.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 13: Vectors
lessons.intention: We are learning to add, subtract and scale vectors in two and three dimensions, find their magnitude and write vectors along a path.
criteria: I can add, subtract and multiply vectors by a number, using components.
I can find the magnitude of a 2D or 3D vector.
I can find the components of AB from the coordinates of A and B.
I can write a vector along a path in terms of other vectors.

steps.start: Ask: from A to B, if you know the vectors OA and OB, which way do you go?
steps.teach: Work component by component. Magnitude is Pythagoras: |v| = √(x² + y² + z²). AB = b − a (B's coordinates take away A's). In a diagram, travel along known vectors: going backwards reverses the sign. In 3D, read coordinates (x, y, z) from a cuboid diagram carefully.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 13: Vectors" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find |AB| for A(1, −2, 3) and B(5, 2, 1).

lessons.home: Describe a route around the house as a sum of vectors.
lessons.vocab: vector, component, magnitude, resultant, 3D coordinates
lessons.understand: Why is AB equal to b − a?
lessons.lookFor: Says from A you go back to O (−a) and then out to B (+b).

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (National 5) 14: Statistics: comparing data and lines of best fit
lessons.intention: We are learning to compare data sets with the mean, median, interquartile range and standard deviation, and to use a line of best fit.
criteria: I can find the standard deviation of a small data set.
I can find quartiles and the interquartile range.
I can compare two data sets in context: one statement on average, one on spread.
I can find the equation of a line of best fit and use it to estimate.

steps.start: Two pupils both average 60%. One scores 58 to 62, the other 30 to 90. Ask: who is more consistent, and how could a number show it?
steps.teach: Standard deviation measures spread about the mean: find the mean, the deviations, square, add, divide by n − 1, square root (the formula is on the formulae list; set out a table). The interquartile range is the upper quartile minus the lower. Comparing: one sentence about the average (mean or median) and one about the spread (standard deviation or IQR), both in context: 'On average… scored higher; …'s scores were more consistent.' Line of best fit: gradient from two points on it, then y = mx + c (or y − b = m(x − a)); use it to estimate.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5) 14: Statistics: comparing data and lines of best fit" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to compare two shops' daily sales given their means and standard deviations.

lessons.home: Time the bus or walk to school for a week and find the mean and standard deviation.
lessons.vocab: mean, standard deviation, quartile, interquartile range, consistent, line of best fit
lessons.understand: Why does a smaller standard deviation mean more consistent?
lessons.lookFor: Says the values are closer to the mean, so they vary less.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb: what the exam expects (National 5)
lessons.intention: We are learning how the National 5 exam is set out and marked: the two papers, what a pass takes, bullet marks and follow-through, and the formulae list.
criteria: I know the papers, their times and their marks.
I know each step of working earns its own mark (one bullet a mark).
I know an error is followed through, so I never leave a question blank.

steps.start: Show an answer with a slip in the middle. Ask how many marks it should keep.
steps.teach: Go through the "What the exam expects: National 5" sheet, then mark its model answers together.
steps.practise: Mark the model answers on the "What the exam expects: National 5" sheet together, then the online mixed exam questions with full working on paper.
steps.check: Ask them to explain follow-through, and what an answer with no working risks.

lessons.home: Do the online mixed exam questions, writing full working on paper.
lessons.vocab: paper, non-calculator, formulae list, bullet mark, follow-through, grade boundary
lessons.understand: Why can a wrong final answer still earn most of a question's marks?
lessons.lookFor: Says each step earns its own bullet, and steps after a slip still count when they're done correctly.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb: mini papers (National 5)
lessons.intention: We are practising exam questions from all the topics together, under exam conditions, and using the results to plan what to revise.
criteria: I can answer mixed exam questions without being told the topic.
I show my working on every question.
I can use my marks to choose which topics to go back to.

steps.start: Recap the habits: read twice, underline the command word, one step a line, round only at the end.
steps.teach: Set up exam conditions: about 20 minutes, quiet, calculator only for the calculator paper. Remind them to do the questions they can first.
steps.practise: One of the "Mini paper: non-calculator (SQA National 5)", "Mini paper: calculator (SQA National 5)" or "Mini paper: longer questions (SQA National 5)" sheets. Each print is a new paper.
steps.check: Mark it together the SQA way, then write the score and the topics to go back to on the tracker.

lessons.home: Redo the questions that lost marks, then the online mixed exam questions.
lessons.vocab: exam conditions, marking, topic, revise
lessons.understand: Your mini paper shows you lost marks on two topics. What do you do next?
lessons.lookFor: Goes back to those topics' lessons or exam sheets before the next mini paper, rather than just doing more papers.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) start here: check and plan
lessons.intention: We are finding out which of the Higher topics are already secure and which to learn first, and making a plan.
criteria: I can try one exam question on each of the 14 Higher topics.
I know which topics I will work on first, and why.
I know how each topic works: lesson, online practice, exam-style sheet, then mini papers.

steps.start: Talk about the goal: Higher. Higher marks come from complete, clearly set-out working on long, multi-part questions.
steps.teach: Explain the stage: 14 topics in order, each with a lesson, online practice and an exam-style sheet; mini papers every few sessions. Do the Higher check (online or on paper), with a calculator but no help: it is a map, not a test.
steps.practise: The "SQA maths climb: Higher check" sheet, or the online Higher check.
steps.check: Mark the check together and fill in the "SQA maths climb: Higher tracker" sheet: the topics that lost marks go first, in climb order.

lessons.home: Look at the tracker together and agree a weekly time for online practice.
lessons.vocab: course, paper, marking instructions, bullet, follow-through, secure
lessons.understand: Why work through the topics in the climb's order rather than starting with the hardest?
lessons.lookFor: Says the early topics are used inside the later ones, so they make the later topics easier as well as earning marks.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 1: The straight line
lessons.intention: We are learning to use gradients, collinearity and perpendicular lines, including medians, altitudes and perpendicular bisectors in triangles.
criteria: I can find a gradient from two points or from an angle (m = tan θ).
I can show points are collinear.
I can find the equation of a line perpendicular to another (m₁ × m₂ = −1).
I can find the equations of medians, altitudes and perpendicular bisectors, and where lines meet.

steps.start: Show a triangle on a grid. Ask: where would you draw the line from a corner to the middle of the opposite side?
steps.teach: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = tan θ, θ measured from the positive x-axis. Collinear: equal gradients and a point in common (say both). Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1. A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side; an altitude is perpendicular to the opposite side through the vertex; a perpendicular bisector goes through a side's midpoint at right angles. Find each with y − b = m(x − a), and solve simultaneously for where two meet.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 1: The straight line" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them for the altitude from C in triangle A(1, 1), B(7, 3), C(2, 8).

lessons.home: Find the steepest street nearby on a map and the angle it makes with the horizontal.
lessons.vocab: gradient, collinear, perpendicular, median, altitude, perpendicular bisector
lessons.understand: What's the difference between a median and an altitude?
lessons.lookFor: Says a median goes to the midpoint of the opposite side; an altitude meets the opposite side at a right angle.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 2: Functions: composite, inverse and domain
lessons.intention: We are learning to form composite functions, find inverse functions and state suitable domains.
criteria: I can find f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) and know they are usually different.
I can find the inverse of a function and know its graph is the reflection in y = x.
I can state a suitable domain (no division by zero, no square root of a negative).

steps.start: Ask: f doubles, g adds 3. Is 'double then add 3' the same as 'add 3 then double'?
steps.teach: f(g(x)) means do g first, then put the result into f: replace every x in f with g(x). To find an inverse, write y = f(x), swap x and y (or rearrange for x), then write f⁻¹(x). The inverse of aˣ is logₐx. A domain excludes values that give division by zero or the square root of a negative.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 2: Functions: composite, inverse and domain" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find f(g(x)) for f(x) = 3x − 1, g(x) = x² + 2, and the inverse of f.

lessons.home: Make a function machine pair (a code and its decoder) and test it on a friend.
lessons.vocab: function, composite, inverse, domain, range
lessons.understand: Why is f(g(x)) usually different from g(f(x))?
lessons.lookFor: Says the order changes what is done first, e.g. (x + 3)² is not x² + 3.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 3: Graphs of functions and transformations
lessons.intention: We are learning to sketch transformations of graphs and to work with exponential and logarithmic graphs.
criteria: I can sketch y = f(x) + a, f(x + a), −f(x), f(−x) and kf(x) from y = f(x).
I can find the image of a point under a transformation.
I can sketch and find the base of exponential and log graphs through a point.

steps.start: Show y = x². Ask where y = (x − 3)² and y = x² − 3 sit.
steps.teach: Changes outside the bracket act on y and do what they say (f(x) + 3 is up 3, 2f(x) doubles heights, −f(x) reflects in the x-axis). Changes inside act on x and do the opposite (f(x − 3) moves right 3, f(−x) reflects in the y-axis). Track the key points (roots, turning points, intercepts) and label them. y = aˣ passes through (0, 1) and (1, a); y = logₐx through (1, 0) and (a, 1).
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 3: Graphs of functions and transformations" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to sketch y = 2 − f(x) for a given f, labelling the images of its turning points.

lessons.home: Sketch a graph, then predict and check its transformations on a free graphing app.
lessons.vocab: transformation, translation, reflection, stretch, exponential, logarithm
lessons.understand: Why does f(x − 3) move the graph right, not left?
lessons.lookFor: Says x has to be 3 bigger to give the same input to f, so every point moves 3 right.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 4: Polynomials and the factor theorem
lessons.intention: We are learning to use synthetic division and the factor theorem to factorise and solve cubic and quartic equations.
criteria: I can use synthetic division to divide a polynomial by (x − a).
I can use the factor and remainder theorems.
I can factorise a cubic fully and solve the equation.
I can find an unknown coefficient from a known factor.

steps.start: Ask: how could you find a factor of x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 without a calculator?
steps.teach: Synthetic division by a: bring the first coefficient down, multiply by a, add, and repeat; the last number is the remainder f(a). Remainder 0 means (x − a) is a factor. Try factors of the constant term. Once one factor is found, the quotient is a quadratic: factorise it, then solve. State 'remainder 0, so (x − a) is a factor': it's a mark.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 4: Polynomials and the factor theorem" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to show (x − 2) is a factor of x³ − 3x² − 4x + 12, then factorise fully.

lessons.home: Write a cubic from three chosen roots, then give it to someone to solve.
lessons.vocab: polynomial, synthetic division, quotient, remainder, factor theorem
lessons.understand: Why are the roots of a cubic among the factors of its constant term (when the x³ coefficient is 1)?
lessons.lookFor: Says the constant is the product of the roots (with signs), so whole-number roots must divide it.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 5: Quadratic theory: discriminant, inequations and tangency
lessons.intention: We are learning to use the discriminant, solve quadratic inequations and show a line is a tangent to a curve.
criteria: I can use the discriminant to find the nature of roots, and conditions for equal, real or no real roots.
I can solve a quadratic inequation with a sketch.
I can show a line is a tangent to a curve and find the point of contact.

steps.start: Ask: how many times can a straight line meet a parabola? Sketch the cases.
steps.teach: b² − 4ac > 0: two real distinct roots; = 0: equal roots; < 0: no real roots; ≥ 0: real roots. Form an inequation for an unknown and solve it (sketch it if it's quadratic). A quadratic inequation: find the roots, sketch the parabola, read the part above or below the axis. Tangency: substitute the line into the curve, rearrange to = 0, show the discriminant is 0 (say 'so the line is a tangent'), then solve for the point.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 5: Quadratic theory: discriminant, inequations and tangency" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them for the values of k for which x² + kx + 9 = 0 has no real roots.

lessons.home: Sketch three lines and a parabola that meet it 0, 1 and 2 times, and write the discriminant condition for each.
lessons.vocab: discriminant, nature of roots, inequation, tangent, point of contact
lessons.understand: Why does a discriminant of 0 mean the line touches the curve?
lessons.lookFor: Says the equation for where they meet has one repeated root, so there is only one meeting point.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 6: Recurrence relations
lessons.intention: We are learning to use linear recurrence relations uₙ₊₁ = auₙ + b, decide when they have a limit, and find it, including in context.
criteria: I can find terms of a recurrence relation.
I can state the condition for a limit (−1 < a < 1).
I can find the limit with L = aL + b.
I can set up and interpret a recurrence relation in context.

steps.start: A pond loses a quarter of its water each week and 100 litres are added. Ask: does it fill up for ever, or settle?
steps.teach: Each term comes from the one before: uₙ₊₁ = auₙ + b. A limit exists only when −1 < a < 1 (write this down: it's a mark). Then L = aL + b, so L = b/(1 − a). In context, a is what is kept (losing 25% keeps 0.75), b what is added; interpret the limit in words and units.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 6: Recurrence relations" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them for the limit of uₙ₊₁ = 0.6uₙ + 12 and what it means in context.

lessons.home: Use a spreadsheet (or calculator's ANS key) to watch a sequence approach its limit.
lessons.vocab: recurrence relation, term, limit, converge
lessons.understand: Why does uₙ₊₁ = 1.2uₙ + 5 have no limit?
lessons.lookFor: Says 1.2 is not between −1 and 1, so the terms keep growing.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 7: Differentiation
lessons.intention: We are learning to differentiate powers (including negative and fractional), use the chain rule, differentiate sin and cos, and find tangents.
criteria: I can rewrite terms as powers of x and differentiate them.
I can find the gradient of a curve at a point.
I can find the equation of a tangent.
I can use the chain rule and differentiate sin ax and cos ax.

steps.start: Ask: how steep is y = x² at x = 3? Zoom in on a graph until it looks straight.
steps.teach: Rewrite first: √x = x^(1/2), 4/x² = 4x⁻². Then multiply by the power and subtract 1. The derivative gives the gradient at a point; a tangent goes through the point with that gradient (find y too), so y − b = m(x − a). Chain rule: differentiate the bracket's power, then multiply by the derivative of the inside. d/dx sin ax = a cos ax, d/dx cos ax = −a sin ax (on the formulae list); x is in radians.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 7: Differentiation" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them for the tangent to y = x³ − 2x at x = 1, and to differentiate (3x − 1)⁵.

lessons.home: Find the speed of a falling ball from its distance formula s = 4.9t² at several times.
lessons.vocab: derivative, gradient, tangent, chain rule, rate of change
lessons.understand: Why must 4/x² be written as 4x⁻² before differentiating?
lessons.lookFor: Says the rule works on powers of x, so the term must be a power first.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 8: Stationary points, optimisation and rates of change
lessons.intention: We are learning to find stationary points and their nature, where a function increases or decreases, and to solve optimisation and rate of change problems.
criteria: I can find stationary points and use a nature table to decide their nature.
I can find where a function is increasing or decreasing.
I can sketch a curve from its stationary points and intercepts.
I can solve optimisation problems with a justification.

steps.start: A pen against a wall uses 40 m of fence. Ask: which width gives the biggest area? Try some.
steps.teach: Stationary points: write dy/dx = 0, solve for x, then find y. A nature table shows the sign of dy/dx just either side: + then − is a maximum, − then + a minimum. Increasing where dy/dx > 0. In optimisation, write the formula in one variable, differentiate, set to 0, and justify it's a maximum or minimum with a nature table before answering in context.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 8: Stationary points, optimisation and rates of change" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find and justify the nature of the stationary points of y = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1.

lessons.home: Make an open box from a square of card by cutting corners; find the best cut by experiment, then by calculus.
lessons.vocab: stationary point, nature table, maximum, minimum, increasing, optimise
lessons.understand: Why do you need a nature table and not just dy/dx = 0?
lessons.lookFor: Says dy/dx = 0 only finds where the slope is flat; the signs either side say whether it's a maximum, minimum or point of inflection.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 9: Integration and area
lessons.intention: We are learning to integrate powers, (ax + b)ⁿ, sin and cos, to evaluate definite integrals, to find areas, and to solve simple differential equations.
criteria: I can integrate powers of x, adding the constant of integration.
I can integrate (ax + b)ⁿ, sin ax and cos ax.
I can evaluate a definite integral and find the area under or between curves.
I can solve dy/dx = f(x) given a point.

steps.start: Ask: what did we differentiate to get 6x? Is there only one answer?
steps.teach: Integration undoes differentiation: add 1 to the power and divide by the new power, and + C for an indefinite integral. (ax + b)ⁿ: raise the power, divide by the new power and by a. ∫cos ax = (1/a) sin ax, ∫sin ax = −(1/a) cos ax. Definite: integrate, put in the top limit minus the bottom. Area below the x-axis comes out negative: give the area as positive, and split at the roots if needed. Between curves: integrate (top − bottom). Given a point, use it to find C.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 9: Integration and area" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them for the area between y = x² − 4x and the x-axis.

lessons.home: Estimate the area under a speed-time graph by counting squares, then by integration.
lessons.vocab: integral, constant of integration, definite, limits, area, differential equation
lessons.understand: Why can a definite integral be negative but an area can't?
lessons.lookFor: Says area below the x-axis gives a negative value; the area is its size, so make it positive.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 10: Radians, exact values and trigonometric equations
lessons.intention: We are learning to use radians and exact values, and to solve trig equations, including with multiple angles and quadratic forms.
criteria: I can change between degrees and radians.
I can give exact values from the special triangles.
I can solve trig equations in degrees or radians in a given interval.
I can solve equations with 2x or 3x, and quadratic trig equations.

steps.start: Ask: sin x = 1/2. How many solutions are there between 0 and 2π?
steps.teach: π radians = 180°. Learn the two special triangles (45°, 45°, 90° and 30°, 60°, 90°) for exact values. To solve: rearrange, find the first angle, use the quadrant diagram for the rest. For sin 2x, solve for 2x over double the interval, then halve. For 2sin²x − sin x − 1 = 0, factorise like a quadratic in sin x, then solve each bracket. Answer in the same units as the interval.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 10: Radians, exact values and trigonometric equations" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to solve 2 cos 2x = 1 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.

lessons.home: Make the two special triangles from card and label every exact value.
lessons.vocab: radian, exact value, interval, quadrant, multiple angle
lessons.understand: Why must you double the interval when solving sin 2x = k?
lessons.lookFor: Says 2x runs over twice the range that x does, so solutions for 2x up to 720° give x up to 360°.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 11: Addition and double angle formulae, and the wave function
lessons.intention: We are learning to use the addition and double angle formulae, prove identities, and write a cos x + b sin x as k cos(x − α).
criteria: I can expand sin(A ± B) and cos(A ± B) and find exact values.
I can use sin 2A and cos 2A in its three forms.
I can write a cos x + b sin x as k cos(x − α) or k sin(x ± α).
I can find the maximum and minimum of a wave function and where they occur.

steps.start: Ask: is sin(30° + 60°) = sin 30° + sin 60°? Check with exact values.
steps.teach: The addition and double angle formulae are on the formulae list: substitute carefully, using a right-angled triangle for the other ratio when given one. For the wave function: expand k cos(x − α) = k cos x cos α + k sin x sin α, compare coefficients (k cos α = a, k sin α = b), k = √(a² + b²), and tan α = b/a in the quadrant given by the signs. The maximum of k cos(x − α) is k, when x = α.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 11: Addition and double angle formulae, and the wave function" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to write cos x − √3 sin x in the form k cos(x − α) with α in degrees.

lessons.home: Use a graphing app to check that 3 cos x + 4 sin x and 5 cos(x − 53.1°) give the same graph.
lessons.vocab: addition formula, double angle, identity, wave function, amplitude
lessons.understand: Why must α's quadrant come from the signs of k cos α and k sin α, not just tan α?
lessons.lookFor: Says tan α is the same in two quadrants, so the signs of cos α and sin α pick the right one.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 12: The circle
lessons.intention: We are learning to use the equation of a circle, find its centre and radius, find tangents, and decide how lines and circles meet.
criteria: I can write the equation of a circle from its centre and radius.
I can find the centre and radius from x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0.
I can find the equation of a tangent at a point on a circle.
I can decide whether circles touch, meet or are apart, and whether a line is a tangent.

steps.start: Ask: which points are exactly 5 from the origin? Plot some.
steps.teach: (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r² has centre (a, b) and radius r. From the general form, the centre is (−g, −f) and r = √(g² + f² − c) (on the formulae list). A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point. Circles: compare the distance between centres with the sum (and difference) of the radii. A line meets a circle where substituting gives a quadratic: its discriminant says 2, 1 (tangent) or 0 points.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 12: The circle" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them for the tangent to x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 12 = 0 at (5, 1).

lessons.home: Use a compass on squared paper to check a circle's equation by plotting points.
lessons.vocab: centre, radius, tangent, general equation, distance
lessons.understand: Why is the tangent's gradient found from the radius's gradient?
lessons.lookFor: Says a tangent meets the radius at a right angle, so their gradients multiply to −1.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 13: Vectors in three dimensions
lessons.intention: We are learning to use vectors in three dimensions: the scalar product, angles between vectors, perpendicular vectors, collinearity and dividing a line.
criteria: I can find the scalar product from components or from |a||b|cos θ.
I can find the angle between two vectors.
I can use a.b = 0 for perpendicular vectors.
I can show points are collinear and find the point dividing a line in a ratio.

steps.start: Ask: how could you find the angle at a corner of a 3D shape you can't measure directly?
steps.teach: a.b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ = |a||b| cos θ (both on the formulae list), so cos θ = a.b / (|a||b|), with both vectors pointing away from the angle. Perpendicular: a.b = 0. Collinear: AB = k BC (parallel) and B is common: say both. A point dividing AB in m : n is A + m/(m + n) AB.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 13: Vectors in three dimensions" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them for the angle between AB and AC for A(1, 0, 2), B(3, 2, 3), C(0, 4, 5).

lessons.home: Find the angle between two edges of a cardboard box from its dimensions.
lessons.vocab: scalar product, magnitude, angle between vectors, perpendicular, collinear, ratio
lessons.understand: Why must both vectors point away from the angle?
lessons.lookFor: Says reversing one vector gives the angle on the other side (180° − θ).

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Higher) 14: Logarithms and exponentials
lessons.intention: We are learning to use the laws of logarithms, solve exponential and log equations, model growth and decay, and use log graphs.
criteria: I can change between logs and exponentials (logₐx = n ⇔ aⁿ = x).
I can use the laws of logs to simplify and evaluate.
I can solve exponential and log equations.
I can model growth and decay and find a formula y = kxⁿ or y = abˣ from a log graph.

steps.start: Ask: 2 to what power is 1000? Between which whole numbers?
steps.teach: logₐx is the power a is raised to give x. Laws: log a + log b = log ab, log a − log b = log(a/b), n log a = log aⁿ, logₐa = 1, logₐ1 = 0. To solve aˣ = b, take logs of both sides. Growth and decay: A = A₀eᵏᵗ; take ln to find k or t. A straight line of log y against log x means y = kxⁿ (gradient n, intercept log k); log y against x means y = abˣ.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher) 14: Logarithms and exponentials" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to solve 5ˣ = 40 and to simplify 2 log₃6 − log₃4.
