lessons.home: Find the half-life of caffeine online and work out how much is left after 10 hours.
lessons.vocab: logarithm, base, exponential, growth, decay, half-life
lessons.understand: Why does taking logs help solve 5ˣ = 40?
lessons.lookFor: Says it brings the unknown power down: x log 5 = log 40.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb: what the exam expects (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning how the Higher exam is set out and marked, and where marks are won and lost: statements, exact values, nature tables and multi-part questions.
criteria: I know the papers, their times and their marks.
I know each step of working earns its own mark (one bullet a mark).
I know an error is followed through, so I never leave a question blank.

steps.start: Show an answer with a slip in the middle. Ask how many marks it should keep.
steps.teach: Go through the "What the exam expects: Higher" sheet, then mark its model answers together.
steps.practise: Mark the model answers on the "What the exam expects: Higher" sheet together, then the online mixed exam questions with full working on paper.
steps.check: Ask them to explain follow-through, and what an answer with no working risks.

lessons.home: Do the online mixed exam questions, writing full working on paper.
lessons.vocab: paper, non-calculator, formulae list, bullet mark, follow-through, grade boundary
lessons.understand: Why can a wrong final answer still earn most of a question's marks?
lessons.lookFor: Says each step earns its own bullet, and steps after a slip still count when they're done correctly.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb: mini papers (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are practising exam questions from all the topics together, under exam conditions, and using the results to plan what to revise.
criteria: I can answer mixed exam questions without being told the topic.
I show my working on every question.
I can use my marks to choose which topics to go back to.

steps.start: Recap the habits: read twice, underline the command word, one step a line, round only at the end.
steps.teach: Set up exam conditions: about 20 minutes, quiet, calculator only for the calculator paper. Remind them to do the questions they can first.
steps.practise: One of the "Mini paper: non-calculator (SQA Higher)", "Mini paper: calculator (SQA Higher)" or "Mini paper: longer questions (SQA Higher)" sheets. Each print is a new paper.
steps.check: Mark it together the SQA way, then write the score and the topics to go back to on the tracker.

lessons.home: Redo the questions that lost marks, then the online mixed exam questions.
lessons.vocab: exam conditions, marking, topic, revise
lessons.understand: Your mini paper shows you lost marks on two topics. What do you do next?
lessons.lookFor: Goes back to those topics' lessons or exam sheets before the next mini paper, rather than just doing more papers.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) start here: check and plan
lessons.intention: We are finding out which of the Advanced Higher topics are already secure and which to learn first, and making a plan.
criteria: I can try one exam question on each of the 14 Advanced Higher topics.
I know which topics I will work on first, and why.
I know how each topic works: lesson, online practice, exam-style sheet, then mini papers.

steps.start: Talk about the goal: Advanced Higher. It builds on Higher's calculus, algebra and vectors, so a slip in a Higher skill costs marks here too.
steps.teach: Explain the stage: 14 topics in order, each with a lesson, online practice and an exam-style sheet; mini papers every few sessions. Do the Advanced Higher check (online or on paper), with a calculator but no help: it is a map, not a test.
steps.practise: The "SQA maths climb: Advanced Higher check" sheet, or the online Advanced Higher check.
steps.check: Mark the check together and fill in the "SQA maths climb: Advanced Higher tracker" sheet: the topics that lost marks go first, in climb order.

lessons.home: Look at the tracker together and agree a weekly time for online practice.
lessons.vocab: course, paper, marking instructions, bullet, follow-through, secure
lessons.understand: Why work through the topics in the climb's order rather than starting with the hardest?
lessons.lookFor: Says the early topics are used inside the later ones, so they make the later topics easier as well as earning marks.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 1: Partial fractions and the binomial theorem
lessons.intention: We are learning to split a rational function into partial fractions and to use the binomial theorem to expand brackets and find a given term.
criteria: I can write a fraction with distinct linear factors as partial fractions.
I can handle a repeated linear factor (A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)²).
I can evaluate a binomial coefficient ⁿCᵣ.
I can find a given term, or the term independent of x, in a binomial expansion.

steps.start: Ask: what is 1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 1) as one fraction? Then ask how you would go backwards.
steps.teach: Partial fractions undo adding fractions. Factorise the bottom, write the form (A/(x − a) + B/(x − b), or A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)² for a repeated factor), multiply through, then substitute the roots or compare coefficients. An improper fraction needs dividing first. The binomial theorem: (a + b)ⁿ = Σ ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ. For a given term, write the general term, collect the powers of x, then choose r.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 1: Partial fractions and the binomial theorem" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to express (5x + 1)/((x − 1)(x + 2)) in partial fractions, and to find the term independent of x in (x + 2/x)⁶.

lessons.home: Build Pascal's triangle to row 8 and check three binomial coefficients from it.
lessons.vocab: partial fractions, proper, improper, repeated factor, binomial coefficient, general term
lessons.understand: Why does a repeated factor (x − 2)² need both A/(x − 2) and B/(x − 2)²?
lessons.lookFor: Says adding fractions over (x − 2) and (x − 2)² can give any linear top over (x − 2)², so both are needed to reach every numerator.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 2: Differentiation: product, quotient and chain rules
lessons.intention: We are learning to differentiate products, quotients and compositions, including eˣ, ln x, and tan, sec, cosec and cot.
criteria: I can use the product rule and the quotient rule.
I can use the chain rule, including more than once.
I can differentiate eˣ, ln x, and functions of them.
I can differentiate tan x, sec x, cosec x and cot x.

steps.start: Ask: is the derivative of x²eˣ just 2x × eˣ? Test it with a graph or a nearby point.
steps.teach: Product rule: (uv)' = u'v + uv'. Quotient rule: (u/v)' = (u'v − uv')/v². Chain rule: differentiate the outside, keep the inside, times the derivative of the inside. (eˣ)' = eˣ and (ln x)' = 1/x. tan x → sec²x, sec x → sec x tan x, cosec x → −cosec x cot x, cot x → −cosec²x (derive them from sin and cos with the quotient rule). Write u, v, u' and v' down before combining: each is a mark.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 2: Differentiation: product, quotient and chain rules" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to differentiate x³ ln x and (2x + 1)/(x − 3).

lessons.home: Prove that the derivative of tan x is sec²x using the quotient rule.
lessons.vocab: product rule, quotient rule, chain rule, exponential, natural logarithm, secant, cosecant, cotangent
lessons.understand: Why does the quotient rule have a minus sign while the product rule has a plus?
lessons.lookFor: Says the bottom's derivative works against the fraction: a bigger bottom makes the fraction smaller, so its term is subtracted.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 3: Implicit, parametric and inverse trig differentiation
lessons.intention: We are learning to differentiate implicitly and parametrically, to differentiate inverse trig functions, and to use derivatives for related rates and motion in a plane.
criteria: I can differentiate an equation in x and y implicitly, using the product rule on xy terms.
I can find dy/dx from parametric equations.
I can differentiate sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ of a function.
I can solve related rates problems and find speed in a plane.

steps.start: Show x² + y² = 25. Ask: how could you find the gradient at (3, 4) without making y the subject?
steps.teach: Implicit: differentiate every term with respect to x; a y term gets × dy/dx (y² → 2y dy/dx), and xy needs the product rule. Collect the dy/dx terms and factorise. Parametric: dy/dx = (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt). Inverse trig: sin⁻¹x → 1/√(1 − x²), tan⁻¹x → 1/(1 + x²), with the chain rule. Related rates: chain the rates together (dV/dt = dV/dr × dr/dt). Speed in a plane: √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²).
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 3: Implicit, parametric and inverse trig differentiation" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them for the gradient of x² + 3xy + y² = 11 at (1, 2), and dy/dx for x = t², y = t³ at t = 2.

lessons.home: Time a filling bottle and use dV/dt to estimate how fast the water level rises.
lessons.vocab: implicit, parametric, parameter, inverse function, related rates, speed
lessons.understand: Why does differentiating y² give 2y dy/dx and not just 2y?
lessons.lookFor: Says y depends on x, so the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of y with respect to x.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 4: Integration: standard results, substitution and partial fractions
lessons.intention: We are learning to integrate with standard results, the f'(x)/f(x) form, partial fractions and a given substitution.
criteria: I can use standard integrals, including 1/(a² + x²) and 1/√(a² − x²).
I can spot and integrate f'(x)/f(x) and g'(f(x))f'(x).
I can integrate a rational function by splitting it into partial fractions.
I can integrate by a given substitution, changing the limits.

steps.start: Ask: which function has derivative 2x/(x² + 1)? How did you know?
steps.teach: Check the list of standard integrals first. If the top is (a multiple of) the derivative of the bottom, ∫ f'(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + c. For a rational function, use partial fractions, then each part gives a ln. For a substitution: write du in terms of dx, change every x (and the limits, for a definite integral), integrate in u, then substitute back or use the new limits. Always + c for an indefinite integral.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 4: Integration: standard results, substitution and partial fractions" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find ∫ 3/(9 + x²) dx and ∫ 1/((x − 1)(x + 3)) dx.

lessons.home: Check an integral by differentiating your answer: you should get back the question.
lessons.vocab: standard integral, substitution, limits, partial fractions, natural logarithm, modulus
lessons.understand: Why do the limits change when you substitute u = x² + 1 in a definite integral?
lessons.lookFor: Says the limits were values of x; once the integral is in u, the limits must be the matching values of u.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 5: Integration by parts, volumes and integration in context
lessons.intention: We are learning to integrate by parts, and to use integration to find volumes of revolution and to solve problems about motion.
criteria: I can integrate by parts, choosing u well, and use it twice if needed.
I can find a volume of revolution about the x-axis or the y-axis.
I can find areas using integration with respect to y.
I can use integration for displacement, velocity and acceleration.

steps.start: Ask: the product rule differentiates uv. What happens if you integrate both sides of it?
steps.teach: ∫ u dv/dx dx = uv − ∫ v du/dx dx. Choose u to be the part that gets simpler when differentiated (a power of x), except with ln x, which is always u. Volume about the x-axis: π∫ y² dx; about the y-axis: π∫ x² dy. Motion: v = ∫ a dt and s = ∫ v dt, using the starting values to find each constant.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 5: Integration by parts, volumes and integration in context" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find ∫ x sin x dx and the volume when y = √x, 0 ≤ x ≤ 4, is rotated about the x-axis.

lessons.home: Use a glass or vase: model its side as a curve and estimate its volume by integration, then check with water.
lessons.vocab: integration by parts, volume of revolution, solid, displacement, velocity, acceleration
lessons.understand: Why is ln x chosen as u in ∫ x ln x dx?
lessons.lookFor: Says ln x is hard to integrate but easy to differentiate (1/x), which makes the second integral simple.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 6: First-order differential equations
lessons.intention: We are learning to solve first-order differential equations by separating the variables or with an integrating factor, and to use them in context.
criteria: I can solve a differential equation with variables separable.
I can find and use an integrating factor for dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x).
I can use a starting condition to find the particular solution.
I can model growth, decay and cooling with a differential equation.

steps.start: Ask: a population grows at a rate proportional to its size. Can you write that as an equation?
steps.teach: Separable: get all the y on one side with dy and all the x on the other with dx, integrate both sides, and put one constant on one side. Linear: write it as dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x); the integrating factor is e^(∫P dx); multiply through, and the left side becomes d/dx(y × the factor). Then integrate and divide. Use the condition to find the constant, and answer the question asked.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 6: First-order differential equations" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to solve dy/dx = 2xy with y = 3 when x = 0, and dy/dx + 2y = 4 with y = 0 when x = 0.

lessons.home: Measure a mug of tea cooling every five minutes and fit Newton's law of cooling to the data.
lessons.vocab: differential equation, separable, integrating factor, general solution, particular solution, initial condition
lessons.understand: Why does the integrating factor make the left side a single derivative?
lessons.lookFor: Says multiplying by e^(∫P dx) makes the left side exactly the product rule result for d/dx(ye^(∫P dx)).

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 7: Second-order differential equations
lessons.intention: We are learning to solve second-order linear differential equations with constant coefficients, homogeneous and non-homogeneous.
criteria: I can write the auxiliary equation and solve it.
I can write the general solution for distinct real, equal and complex roots.
I can find a particular integral and add it to the complementary function.
I can use two conditions to find both constants.

steps.start: Ask: what number m makes y = eᵐˣ a solution of d²y/dx² − 5dy/dx + 6y = 0?
steps.teach: Try y = eᵐˣ: the auxiliary equation am² + bm + c = 0. Distinct real roots p, q: y = Aeᵖˣ + Beᑫˣ. Equal roots p: y = (A + Bx)eᵖˣ. Complex roots α ± βi: y = e^(αx)(A cos βx + B sin βx). Non-homogeneous: the general solution is the complementary function plus a particular integral, found by trying the same type as the right side (a constant, ax + b, ae^(kx), or a cos + b sin). Use the two conditions last, on the full solution.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 7: Second-order differential equations" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to solve d²y/dx² + 4y = 0 with y = 1 and dy/dx = 2 when x = 0.

lessons.home: Use a spring or pendulum video to discuss why complex roots give oscillation.
lessons.vocab: auxiliary equation, complementary function, particular integral, homogeneous, general solution
lessons.understand: Why do complex roots give sines and cosines?
lessons.lookFor: Says e^(iβx) = cos βx + i sin βx, so the real solutions are combinations of cos βx and sin βx (times e^(αx)).

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 8: Functions and graphs: asymptotes, odd and even, modulus
lessons.intention: We are learning to find asymptotes, decide whether functions are odd or even, find points of inflection and sketch related graphs, including the modulus function.
criteria: I can find vertical, horizontal and slant asymptotes of a rational function.
I can show a function is odd, even or neither using f(−x).
I can find points of inflection and stationary points.
I can sketch |f(x)|, f⁻¹(x) and f'(x) from the graph of f(x).

steps.start: Show y = 1/x. Ask: what happens as x gets near 0, and as x gets very large?
steps.teach: Vertical asymptotes are where the bottom is zero (and the top isn't). As x → ±∞, divide to find the horizontal or slant asymptote: if the top's degree is one more than the bottom's, there is a slant asymptote y = mx + c. Even: f(−x) = f(x) (symmetric in the y-axis); odd: f(−x) = −f(x) (rotational symmetry about the origin). A point of inflection is where the concavity changes: f''(x) = 0 and changes sign. |f(x)| reflects the parts below the x-axis.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 8: Functions and graphs: asymptotes, odd and even, modulus" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them for the asymptotes of y = (2x² + 3x)/(x − 1), and whether x³ sin x is odd or even.

lessons.home: Sketch y = (x² + 1)/x by hand, then check with graphing software.
lessons.vocab: asymptote, slant asymptote, odd, even, point of inflection, modulus, concavity
lessons.understand: Why is f''(x) = 0 not enough to prove a point of inflection?
lessons.lookFor: Says f''(x) must change sign there too: y = x⁴ has f''(0) = 0 but a minimum, not an inflection.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 9: Sequences, series and Maclaurin expansions
lessons.intention: We are learning to work with arithmetic and geometric sequences and series, sums to infinity, summation formulae and Maclaurin expansions.
criteria: I can find the nth term and the sum of n terms of an arithmetic or geometric series.
I can find a sum to infinity and state when it exists.
I can use Σr, Σr² and Σr³ formulae.
I can find a Maclaurin expansion and combine expansions.

steps.start: Ask: if you keep adding half of what's left (1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + …), where do you end up?
steps.teach: Arithmetic: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d and Sₙ = n/2(2a + (n − 1)d). Geometric: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹ and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r); the sum to infinity a/(1 − r) exists only when −1 < r < 1. Σr = n(n + 1)/2, Σr² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, Σr³ = n²(n + 1)²/4. Maclaurin: f(x) = f(0) + f'(0)x + f''(0)x²/2! + f'''(0)x³/3! + …; combine known expansions by multiplying or substituting.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 9: Sequences, series and Maclaurin expansions" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them for the sum to infinity of 12 + 8 + 16/3 + …, and the first three terms of the Maclaurin expansion of e^(2x).

lessons.home: Use a spreadsheet to add the terms of a geometric series and watch it approach its limit.
lessons.vocab: arithmetic, geometric, common difference, common ratio, sum to infinity, convergent, Maclaurin series
lessons.understand: Why does a geometric series with r = 2 have no sum to infinity?
lessons.lookFor: Says the terms get bigger and bigger, so the total grows without limit.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 10: Proof and number theory
lessons.intention: We are learning to prove and disprove statements, using counterexamples, direct proof, contradiction and induction, and to use Euclid's algorithm and number bases.
criteria: I can disprove a statement with a counterexample and write a negation.
I can write a direct proof, a proof by contradiction or by the contrapositive.
I can write a full proof by induction.
I can use Euclid's algorithm, write the gcd as a linear combination, and change number bases.

steps.start: Ask: n² + n + 41 is prime for n = 0, 1, 2, 3, … Is it always prime? How would you know?
steps.teach: One counterexample disproves an 'all' statement. The negation swaps ∀ and ∃ and negates the condition. Direct proof: start from what you know and reason step by step (an even number is 2k, an odd number 2k + 1). Contradiction: assume the opposite and reach something impossible (√2 is irrational). Induction: prove it for n = 1; assume it for n = k; show it then holds for n = k + 1; write the conclusion. Euclid's algorithm: divide, keep the remainder, repeat; the last non-zero remainder is the gcd; work back up to write it as ax + by.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 10: Proof and number theory" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to prove by induction that 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n², and to find gcd(252, 198).

lessons.home: Find a famous conjecture that held for millions of cases and then failed.
lessons.vocab: conjecture, counterexample, negation, contradiction, contrapositive, induction, greatest common divisor, base
lessons.understand: Why does a proof by induction need both the first case and the step from k to k + 1?
lessons.lookFor: Says the first case starts the chain and the step lets each case push over the next, like dominoes; without either, the chain breaks.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 11: Matrices: products, determinants, inverses and transformations
lessons.intention: We are learning to multiply matrices, find determinants and inverses, decide when a matrix is singular, and use 2 × 2 matrices for transformations.
criteria: I can add and multiply matrices up to order 3, and know AB ≠ BA in general.
I can find the determinant of a 2 × 2 and a 3 × 3 matrix.
I can find the inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix and know when a matrix is singular.
I can write and combine 2 × 2 transformation matrices.

steps.start: Ask: does multiplying matrices work like multiplying numbers? Try AB and BA for two 2 × 2 matrices.
steps.teach: Multiply rows of the first by columns of the second. det of (a, b; c, d) is ad − bc; for a 3 × 3, expand along a row with the signs + − +. A matrix with determinant 0 is singular: it has no inverse. The 2 × 2 inverse is 1/(ad − bc) × (d, −b; −c, a). Transformation matrices: the columns are the images of (1, 0) and (0, 1). Combining: the transformation done first goes on the right. det(AB) = det A × det B.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 11: Matrices: products, determinants, inverses and transformations" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the inverse of the matrix with rows (3, 1) and (5, 2), and the matrix for a 90° rotation then a reflection in the x-axis.

lessons.home: Draw a shape, apply a matrix to its corners, and see how its area changes compared with the determinant.
lessons.vocab: matrix, order, determinant, singular, inverse, identity, transpose, transformation
lessons.understand: Why does a singular matrix have no inverse?
lessons.lookFor: Says its determinant is 0, so 1/det can't be found; the transformation squashes the plane flat, so it can't be undone.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 12: Systems of equations: Gaussian elimination
lessons.intention: We are learning to solve three equations in three unknowns by Gaussian elimination, and to recognise when there is no solution, infinitely many, or ill-conditioning.
criteria: I can write a system as an augmented matrix.
I can use row operations to reach upper triangular form and back-substitute.
I can find when a system has no unique solution, and say whether it has none or infinitely many.
I can explain ill-conditioning.

steps.start: Ask: two equations in two unknowns have one solution, none, or infinitely many. What does each look like on a graph?
steps.teach: Write the augmented matrix. Use row operations (swap rows, multiply a row, add a multiple of one row to another) to get zeros below the leading diagonal. Then solve from the bottom row up. A bottom row of 0 0 0 | k with k ≠ 0 means no solution (inconsistent); 0 0 0 | 0 means infinitely many. Ill-conditioned: a tiny change in a coefficient makes a big change in the answer, as the planes (or lines) are nearly parallel.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 12: Systems of equations: Gaussian elimination" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to solve x + y + z = 6, 2x − y + z = 3, x + 2y − z = 2.

lessons.home: Use software to solve a system, then change one number slightly and compare the answers.
lessons.vocab: augmented matrix, row operation, upper triangular, back-substitution, inconsistent, ill-conditioned
lessons.understand: What does a row 0 0 0 | 5 tell you?
lessons.lookFor: Says it means 0 = 5, which is impossible, so the system has no solution.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 13: Vectors: the vector product, lines and planes
lessons.intention: We are learning to use the vector product and the scalar triple product, and the equations of lines and planes in three dimensions.
criteria: I can find a × b and use it for a vector perpendicular to two others.
I can find the equation of a plane in Cartesian, vector or parametric form.
I can find where a line meets a plane, and whether two lines intersect.
I can find the angle between two planes, or a line and a plane.

steps.start: Ask: how could you find a vector at right angles to both edges of a sloping roof?
steps.teach: a × b is the determinant with i, j, k on the top row; it is perpendicular to a and b, and |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ. The scalar triple product a.(b × c) is a volume. A plane with normal n through A: n.r = n.a, i.e. ax + by + cz = d. For three points, the normal is AB × AC. A line r = a + td meets a plane where substituting gives t. The angle between planes is the angle between their normals; between a line and a plane it is 90° minus the angle to the normal.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 13: Vectors: the vector product, lines and planes" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them for the equation of the plane through (1, 0, 2), (2, 1, 0) and (0, 3, 1).

lessons.home: Use a book and pencils to model two planes and their line of intersection.
lessons.vocab: vector product, normal, plane, Cartesian equation, parametric, scalar triple product
lessons.understand: Why is AB × AC normal to the plane ABC?
lessons.lookFor: Says the vector product is perpendicular to both AB and AC, which both lie in the plane.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb (Advanced Higher) 14: Complex numbers and de Moivre's theorem
lessons.intention: We are learning to calculate with complex numbers, use the Argand diagram, modulus and argument, de Moivre's theorem and complex roots of polynomials.
criteria: I can add, subtract, multiply and divide complex numbers.
I can find the modulus and argument and write z in polar form.
I can use de Moivre's theorem for powers and nth roots.
I can solve polynomials with a given complex root, and describe loci in the Argand diagram.

steps.start: Ask: x² = −1 has no real solution. What if we invent a number i with i² = −1?
steps.teach: Treat i like a letter, replacing i² with −1. To divide, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom. On the Argand diagram, |z| is the distance from 0 and arg z the angle from the positive real axis (−π < arg z ≤ π; check the quadrant). Polar form z = r(cos θ + i sin θ); de Moivre: zⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ). A real polynomial's complex roots come in conjugate pairs. |z − a| = r is a circle centre a, radius r.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Advanced Higher) 14: Complex numbers and de Moivre's theorem" sheet, marked the SQA way (one bullet a mark, errors followed through), then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to express (3 + 2i)/(1 − i) in the form a + bi, and to find (1 + i)⁸.

lessons.home: Plot z, iz, i²z and i³z for one z and describe what multiplying by i does.
lessons.vocab: complex number, real part, imaginary part, conjugate, modulus, argument, Argand diagram, polar form
lessons.understand: Why do complex roots of a polynomial with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs?
lessons.lookFor: Says taking the conjugate of the whole equation leaves the real coefficients unchanged, so the conjugate of a root is a root too.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb: what the exam expects (Advanced Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning how the Advanced Higher exam is set out and marked, and where marks are won and lost: naming the method, constants of integration, full proofs and exact answers.
criteria: I know the papers, their times and their marks.
I know each step of working earns its own mark (one bullet a mark).
I know an error is followed through, so I never leave a question blank.

steps.start: Show an answer with a slip in the middle. Ask how many marks it should keep.
steps.teach: Go through the "What the exam expects: Advanced Higher" sheet, then mark its model answers together.
steps.practise: Mark the model answers on the "What the exam expects: Advanced Higher" sheet together, then the online mixed exam questions with full working on paper.
steps.check: Ask them to explain follow-through, and what an answer with no working risks.

lessons.home: Do the online mixed exam questions, writing full working on paper.
lessons.vocab: paper, non-calculator, formulae list, bullet mark, follow-through, grade boundary
lessons.understand: Why can a wrong final answer still earn most of a question's marks?
lessons.lookFor: Says each step earns its own bullet, and steps after a slip still count when they're done correctly.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb: mini papers (Advanced Higher)
lessons.intention: We are practising exam questions from all the topics together, under exam conditions, and using the results to plan what to revise.
criteria: I can answer mixed exam questions without being told the topic.
I show my working on every question.
I can use my marks to choose which topics to go back to.

steps.start: Recap the habits: read twice, underline the command word, one step a line, round only at the end.
steps.teach: Set up exam conditions: about 20 minutes, quiet, calculator only for the calculator paper. Remind them to do the questions they can first.
steps.practise: One of the "Mini paper: non-calculator (SQA Advanced Higher)", "Mini paper: calculator (SQA Advanced Higher)" or "Mini paper: longer questions (SQA Advanced Higher)" sheets. Each print is a new paper.
steps.check: Mark it together the SQA way, then write the score and the topics to go back to on the tracker.

lessons.home: Redo the questions that lost marks, then the online mixed exam questions.
lessons.vocab: exam conditions, marking, topic, revise
lessons.understand: Your mini paper shows you lost marks on two topics. What do you do next?
lessons.lookFor: Goes back to those topics' lessons or exam sheets before the next mini paper, rather than just doing more papers.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb: exam technique, command words and setting out
lessons.intention: We are learning what each SQA command word asks for, and to set out working so every step can be given its mark.
criteria: I know what state, evaluate, solve, express in the form, hence, show that, justify and determine the nature ask for.
I set out working one step a line.
I write the statements that earn marks on their own.

steps.start: Show 'Hence solve…' after a part (a). Ask what 'hence' tells them to do.
steps.teach: Go through the command words on the "SQA exam technique: command words and setting out" sheet. Show how a marking scheme gives one bullet a step, so a step that isn't written can't be marked.
steps.practise: The "SQA exam technique: command words and setting out" sheet: three questions set out step by step, then compared with the marking.
steps.check: Ask them what 'show that' and 'justify your answer' each need.

lessons.home: Pick any three online exam questions and write out the working as bullets before checking.
lessons.vocab: command word, hence, show that, justify, nature, sketch
lessons.understand: Why is writing 'dy/dx = 0' worth a mark even though it's obvious?
lessons.lookFor: Says the marker can only give marks for what is written, and that statement is the strategy step.
lessons.sqa: National 5, Higher and Advanced Higher Mathematics

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA maths climb: my next step (working on your own, National 5 to Advanced Higher)
lessons.intention: We are learning to follow the climb on our own: take the check, practise the next topic, mark our work the SQA way and know when to move on.
criteria: I can open the climb page and follow My next step.
I read the marking after every question, even when I was right.
I can mark my own working one bullet a step.
I know when a topic is secure and when to move to the next stage.

steps.start: Ask: when you study on your own, how do you decide what to do next? Talk about why guessing wastes time.
steps.teach: Open popspell.com/climb.html?course=sqa together. Show My next step: it starts with the stage check, then picks the first topic that needs work, in the climb's order, and suggests a mini paper when a stage is nearly done. Show where the marking appears after each answer and how a topic becomes secure (three-quarters of the marks on a practice set). Explain that progress stays on this device only.
steps.practise: The "SQA maths climb: my route from National 5 to Advanced Higher" sheet: fill in the exam and target together, then do one practice set on the climb page.
steps.check: Ask them to show you their next step on the climb page and explain why that topic comes next.

lessons.home: Two or three sessions a week on the climb page, about 45 minutes each, with a notebook for working.
lessons.vocab: self-guided, marking, secure, stage, next step
lessons.understand: Why read the marking even when you got the answer right?
lessons.lookFor: Says it shows which steps earn marks, so you can write them in the exam even when the last step goes wrong.
lessons.sqa: National 5, Higher and Advanced Higher Mathematics
